introduction: “Day and night we must think and plan how to become more self-sacrificing in the Path of God.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá wrote these letters to people who had left homes and occupations to carry a message from town to town and across oceans, and he does not ask them for moderation: seek not a moment’s rest; make teaching “the sole object and entire concern” of life; without service “life itself is meaningless.” The later readings, from Shoghi Effendi’s letters, draw the practical conclusion that devotion matters more to a teacher than knowledge, because it is what attracts confirmation. The model ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names is the apostles, and so Paul is quoted often: his journeys, his “one thing I do,” his “spend and be spent.” Jeremiah’s fire in the bones, the Qur’án’s “my living and my dying are for Allah,” and the grain of wheat that must fall into the ground belong with them. Three passages raise the question a reader may already be asking: Jesus told his overworked disciples to rest a while; a psalm calls sleepless labour vain; and Milton, blind, found that “they also serve who only stand and wait.”
questions: “Let every soul make the sole object and entire concern of his being nothing less than the teaching of the Faith.” How could that be true of a person with a job and a family?
The readings say “seek not a moment’s rest”; Jesus said “rest a while.” How do you hold the two?
“Knowledge is, of course essential; but compared to devotion it is secondary.” Why might a devoted teacher with little learning succeed where a learned one does not?
Milton: “They also serve who only stand and wait.” What forms can devotion take for someone who cannot travel or speak?
“Seeking each day how to bring some of the spirit of life to a seeker.” What would that look like tomorrow?

outside.why: “Day and night we must think and plan how to become more self-sacrificing in the Path of God.” Paul: present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
A wife and husband are to serve “in unison.” Paul’s greeting to such a couple: Priscilla and Aquila my helpers, who have for my life laid down their own necks.

“You made such a commitment … I am always awaiting good news.” The letter to Ephesus, a hard-working church: nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love. How is a commitment kept alive after its first enthusiasm?
“Today, each and every one … must focus their thoughts on teaching.” Jesus: I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
They have “devoted yourselves to sacrifice.” Paul: I will very gladly spend and be spent for you.
“Dedicate your lives to the service of the Beloved.” The Qur’án: my worship and my sacrifice and my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the Worlds.
Let every soul make teaching “the sole object and entire concern of his being.” Paul: this one thing I do; I press toward the mark.
Paul on how little choice he felt he had: necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
“Our aim is not to rest but to … serve.” Jesus, pressed to eat: my meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work.
“Seek not a moment’s rest … Open thy tongue.” Paul to Timothy: preach the word; be instant in season, out of season.

Jesus, when his disciples had no leisure so much as to eat: come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while. Is there a place for rest in a devoted life? Where would these readings put it?
“We must sacrifice our comfort for Him.” Jesus: let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.

Otherwise “God will raise up souls to do this work in our stead.” Milton, blind and unable to do the work he had planned, concluded differently: God doth not need either man’s work, or His own gifts; they also serve who only stand and wait. What would the readings say to someone who cannot go out and teach?
Friends who have “forsaken their physical comfort and ease, and have gone from city to city.” Peter: lo, we have left all, and have followed thee.
A teacher who left his country and accepted hardships. Paul: in journeyings often, in perils of waters, in weariness and painfulness.
“You … sacrificed your life and wealth in the love of God.” Paul: I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.
“Through his zeal, he will sacrifice everything.” Jeremiah, when he tried to stop: his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I could not stay.
Friends “ready at every moment to sacrifice their lives.” Paul: neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy.

Believers “have accepted happily chains and fetters” to promote the teachings. Jesus: except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
“How sweet … when a true lover sacrifices his life in the path of the Beloved.” The psalmist: the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
“Consider what the Disciples … did by throwing away comfort and rest.” Paul reminds the Ephesians: by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
The apostles made a pact to bear tribulation and spread guidance. Paul on how they did it: we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls.
“These souls know no rest—they strive night and day.” Ecclesiastes: whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.

A psalm sounds a caution about work without rest: it is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep. And Jethro told Moses he would wear himself out. What keeps devotion from becoming exhaustion?
Knowledge is essential, “but compared to devotion it is secondary.” Paul ranks them the same way: though I understand all mysteries, and all knowledge, and have not charity, I am nothing.
“The brighter our torch burns, the more light will it give.” Jesus: neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
To “become a reed through which the Holy Spirit” speaks. Rúmí’s reed, cut from its bed, has nothing of its own to say: hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains.
Seeking “each day how to bring some of the spirit of life to a seeker.” Tennyson’s Ulysses, on a life kept in use: how dull it is to pause, to make an end, to rust unburnish’d, not to shine in use!
